forces: Double string orchestra and string quartet
performers: The U.S. Army Strings, U.S. Army Band “Pershing’s Own”
intro: Two string orchestras and a solo quartet answer one another through a sixteenth-century psalm tune. The U.S. Army Strings play the Fantasia that Vaughan Williams first conducted in Gloucester Cathedral in 1910.

cues.title: Chords, then plucked fragments
cues.text: Soft descending chords open the work. Then the low strings pluck the first fragments of Tallis’s tune, answered by a swaying phrase on the bowed strings that returns again and again as a refrain.
cues.evidence: Steve Schwartz’s listening guide to the Fantasia (Classical Net) describes the opening chords, the plucked fragments in the low strings and the swaying figure that recurs as a refrain. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The whole tune, in unison
cues.text: All the strings join for the first full statement of Tallis’s tune. Second violins, violas and first cellos play the melody in unison, one line with the weight of a choir. Rising runs later hand it to the first violins and violas, playing in octaves.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: in the statement the second violins, violas and first cellos carry the melody in unison, and after rising arpeggios it returns in the first violins and first violas with octave double-stopping. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gloucester Cathedral, 6 September 1910
cues.text: The Fantasia was first played in Gloucester Cathedral on 6 September 1910, to about two thousand people who had come mostly for Elgar’s Gerontius. The cathedral’s organist, Herbert Brewer, called it “a queer, mad work by an odd fellow from Chelsea”.
cues.evidence: Terry Blain, BBC Music Magazine (classical-music.com), 10 April 2025, and Rob Young, The Guardian, 12 June 2010: audience, programme and Brewer’s remark. https://www.classical-music.com/features/works/vaughan-williams-tallis-fantasia-premiere ; https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2010/jun/12/vaughan-williams-fantasia-theme-tallis

cues.title: First episode: orchestras divide
cues.text: In the first episode a blunt, declamatory phrase from Tallis alternates with the swaying chords. The small second orchestra later takes the soft descending chords of the opening, and the large orchestra answers with the sway.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: in the first episode an abrupt statement of the second Tallis phrase alternates with the sway, then the opening chords return in orchestra II against the sway in orchestra I. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune from Archbishop Parker
cues.text: The theme is the third of nine tunes Tallis wrote for Archbishop Parker’s Psalter of 1567, set to Psalm 2. Vaughan Williams met it while editing The English Hymnal, where it carries Addison’s hymn “When rising from the bed of death”.
cues.evidence: IMSLP work page for the Fantasia (“Third Tune (Psalm 2)” of 9 Tunes for Archbishop Parker’s Psalter); Schwartz’s guide (English Hymnal no. 92, Addison’s hymn); Terry Blain, BBC Music Magazine, 2025. https://imslp.org/wiki/Fantasia_on_a_Theme_by_Thomas_Tallis_(Vaughan_Williams,_Ralph)

cues.title: Solo viola leads off
cues.text: A solo viola opens the second episode with a variation on the tune’s rising Phrygian phrase. The rest of the solo quartet join it, and the tune is passed from one player to the next in a quiet polyphonic meditation.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: the solo viola leads off the second episode with a variant of the third Tallis phrase, which the string quartet takes up. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The quartet takes over
cues.text: The solo quartet of two violins, viola and cello takes up the phrase, and both orchestras answer in bold, declaimed statements. The quartet then carries on its polyphonic meditation before the large orchestra declaims the phrase once more.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: the string quartet takes up the third phrase, the orchestras answer with declamations, and the quartet continues its “polyphonic meditation”. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third episode begins the build
cues.text: The third episode works on the swaying figure. The small orchestra extends the quartet’s sway, then both orchestras start the long build to the largest climax of the work.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: the third episode explores the swaying subject; the two orchestras “begin to build to a huge climax” culminating in the third phrase. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The great climax
cues.text: The build peaks in the biggest climax of the piece, on the rising phrase of the tune. Afterwards the sound dies away to the small second orchestra, an afterglow before the hush of the fourth episode.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: the third episode builds to “a huge climax, culminating in A3”, then dies down to an “afterglow” in the small orchestra. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sway cannot get going
cues.text: In the fourth episode the swaying chords try to start again but cannot get beyond two notes. They dissolve into fragments of the opening chords.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: in the fourth episode the sway “doesn’t seem to be able to get beyond two notes” and dissolves into fragments of the opening chords. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tallis’s tune, plucked again
cues.text: The lower strings pluck out Tallis’s tune once more over a cushion of sustained sound. A solo violin and viola share the later phrases with the swaying chords, and the full strings join for the last phrase.
cues.evidence: Schwartz’s guide: in the restatement the lower strings pluck the hymn again over a “featherbed of sound”, a solo violin and viola duet on the later phrases, and everybody joins for the fourth. http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Howells in the audience
cues.text: A seventeen-year-old Herbert Howells heard the first performance. Seventy-one years later he called the evening “so disturbing and moving that I even asked RVW for his autograph – and got it!” He and Ivor Gurney walked the streets of Gloucester half the night.
cues.evidence: Rob Young, “Cloud of knowing”, The Guardian, 12 June 2010, quoting Howells’s recollection of 1981; Terry Blain, BBC Music Magazine, 2025. https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2010/jun/12/vaughan-williams-fantasia-theme-tallis

cues.title: Coda: the quartet, then a last chord
cues.text: In the coda the solo quartet sings the last phrases, marked p espr., and the orchestras slow together. The final chord is struck ff and held under a pause, fading to pppp.
cues.evidence: Steve Schwartz’s guide: “the strings carry the sway to the end, with a short benediction”: http://www.classical.net/music/comp.lst/works/v-w/tallisfantasia.php. Vaughan Williams, Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis, Boosey & Hawkes pocket score (1921), p. 21: “Soli”, p espr., “molto rit.”, then the final chord marked ff, held under a fermata and diminishing to pppp: https://archive.org/details/fantasiaonthemeb00vaug
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Commons credits the artist as “Orchestra d’archi dell’esercito degli Stati Uniti”; the archived Army Band download page is headed The U.S. Army Band “Pershing’s Own” – Army Strings Audio Downloads. Neither names a conductor or soloist. IMSLP lists a 14:53 recording from the U.S. Army Band (uploaded 2010) with the U.S. Army Strings under Lt. Col. John Clanton; the Commons page does not confirm that it is the same file.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The Commons description says only “Fantasia su un tema di Thomas Tallis”. Which of the 1910, 1913 and 1919 versions is played, the performing edition and the number of players in each group are not stated.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives “circa 2010” for the file. That is the uploader’s date for the recording, not a documented session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The ensemble’s home base does not establish the recording venue.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The file came from the U.S. Army Band’s own download page, not from a commercial label.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix, take or original carrier is identified; the digital file alone does not settle whether such identifiers exist.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Imported to Wikimedia Commons from Italian Wikipedia (FileImporter); original source: the U.S. Army Band download page.
fields.note: The Commons import comment and the Credit field give this chain. No personal mastering credit is stated.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons file timestamp (4 October 2012) is an import date, not a transfer or session date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Ogg Vorbis file with an MP3 access derivative supplied by Wikimedia Commons.
fields.note: Earlier processing by the Army Band (its page offered MP3 files compressed in zip format) is not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Vaughan Williams’s copyright in the music runs to the end of 2028 in the UK and EU; the Fantasia (first published 1921) is in the public domain in the United States and Canada.
fields.note: The Vaughan Williams Foundation gives 2028 as the year copyright in his music expires; IMSLP records the work as public domain in Canada and the United States and not in countries with life plus 70 years. Any modern edition has its own rights.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Public domain, as declared on the Wikimedia Commons file page.
fields.note: The licence status is declared on the file page, but the template used there ({{PD-Old}}) concerns the age of the composition, which cannot apply to Vaughan Williams’s music in the UK or EU, and says nothing about the recording. The likely basis is that a U.S. Army Band recording is a work of the U.S. government; neither the file page nor the archived Army Band page says so. IMSLP lists the 14:53 Army Strings recording under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0.

composer.epithet: He wrote down an Essex folk song in 1903, edited the English Hymnal and carried a Tudor psalm tune into the concert hall.

Composer, folk-song collector, hymn-book editor, teacher and conductor; Leith Hill Musical Festival, 1905–53
Gustav Holst · Adeline and Ursula Vaughan Williams · Adrian Boult · Hubert Foss at Oxford University Press
Nine symphonies, operas, a masque for dancing, choral works, songs, hymn tunes, film scores and music for amateurs

quote.text: In the next world, I shan’t be doing music, with all the striving and disappointments. I shall be being it.
quote.source: Vaughan Williams to Sylvia Townsend Warner, about a fortnight before his death in August 1958, as she recorded it in a letter

composer.background:
On 9 February 1875 Arthur Vaughan Williams, vicar of All Saints, Down Ampney, died after a brief illness. His third child, Ralph, born in the vicarage on 12 October 1872, was two. His widow Margaret, a Wedgwood, took the children to her family’s house at Leith Hill Place in Surrey. Aunt Sophy gave the boy piano lessons, and at six he wrote a piece called The Robin’s Nest. He went to Charterhouse in 1887 and to the Royal College of Music in 1890, where Hubert Parry taught him composition; in 1892 he went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, to read history as well as music.

Adeline Fisher, a cellist and pianist whose first cousin was Virginia Woolf, became his wife on 9 October 1897 at All Saints, Hove, three days before his twenty-fifth birthday. After a brief spell of study with Max Bruch in Berlin he went back to his post as organist at St Barnabas, South Lambeth, which he had held since 1895, disliked, and gave up in 1899.
